articles.excerpt: Google Gemini now provides two first-party ways to turn a natural-language prompt into a working web experience. Gemini Canvas is designed for rapid visual prototyping inside the Gemini interface, whi…
articles.body: Google Gemini now provides two first-party ways to turn a natural-language prompt into a working web experience. Gemini Canvas is designed for rapid visual prototyping inside the Gemini interface, while Build mode in Google AI Studio generates a code-backed, full-stack web app that can be refined, shared, exported, or deployed to Google Cloud Run. The distinction matters for businesses that want to test an idea quickly without treating every early experiment as a finished software product. Canvas can help turn a concept into a shareable prototype in minutes. AI Studio Build mode offers a more direct route from the same kind of prompt to an editable application codebase and a live deployment workflow.

articles.title: I checked my product links logged out. Most of them were login walls.
articles.excerpt: I sell a small writing service. For about a week it had zero orders, and I assumed nobody wanted it. So I rewrote the description. Twice. Then I opened my own links in a private window. Every link I h…
articles.body: I sell a small writing service. For about a week it had zero orders, and I assumed nobody wanted it. So I rewrote the description. Twice. Then I opened my own links in a private window. Every link I had handed out showed a sign-in screen. My listing, my checkout, the "public example" I had submitted to a directory. A stranger without an account could not read the offer, let alone buy it. I had spent days rewriting the copy on a door nobody could open. If you ship anything with a share link, this is a ten minute check. Check the link, not the status code curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/your-listing Careful. 200 is not proof. Plenty of apps return 200 with a login page.

articles.title: Why catch-all email addresses can't be verified (and what to do instead)
articles.excerpt: If you've ever run a list through an email verifier, you've probably seen a result labelled catch-all, accept-all or unknown. It's tempting to treat that as a bug in the tool. It isn't. It's a hard li…
articles.body: If you've ever run a list through an email verifier, you've probably seen a result labelled catch-all , accept-all or unknown . It's tempting to treat that as a bug in the tool. It isn't. It's a hard limit of how email works, and once you understand it you'll make better decisions about what to send to. How verification works under the hood A verifier never sends an email. It runs a short conversation with the recipient's mail server and stops just before the message would be delivered: Syntax check. Is anna@example.com even a well-formed address? DNS lookup. Does example.com publish MX records, i.e. does anything accept mail for this domain? SMTP handshake.

articles.title: GROUP BY In PostgreSQL
articles.excerpt: For a while, GROUP BY was basically the ceiling of what I knew how to do with aggregation. Total per city, count per venue, that kind of thing. Then I ran into a task — rank venues within their own ci…
articles.body: For a while, GROUP BY was basically the ceiling of what I knew how to do with aggregation. Total per city, count per venue, that kind of thing. Then I ran into a task — rank venues within their own city by latitude, but keep every single venue row in the result, not collapse them into one row per city — and GROUP BY just couldn't do it. That's the gap window functions fill, and once it clicked, a bunch of queries that used to feel awkward got a lot simpler. What GROUP BY can't do GROUP BY collapses rows. If you group venues by city and count them, you get one row per city — the individual venues are gone from the result, folded into that count. That's exactly what you want sometimes.

articles.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission
articles.excerpt: Victor Glover recalls how a suspected cabin leak warning came just 15 minutes before a crucial engine burn — and why receiving it just five minutes later could have changed everything.
articles.body: TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission. "If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife. The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away.

articles.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
articles.excerpt: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia.
articles.body: A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape.

articles.title: Next Mass Effect game cancelled as EA shuts down legendary sci-fi RPG studio BioWare
articles.excerpt: The legendary RPG studio behind classics such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age is no more.
articles.body: The writing was on the wall, but the news still hit us like a truck yesterday. BioWare, the iconic RPG studio behind the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series, is no more. Development on the next Mass Effect has stopped, but EA might not be entirely done with the IP. Variety reported, backed by EA’s own statement and BioWare’s goodbye on socials , that EA is laying off 3% of its global workforce and closing down BioWare. The shift comes shortly after the company went fully private this summer , with Saudi Arabia and private equity acquiring it alongside all its studios and properties.

articles.title: NASA giving update about Artemis moon plans on Oct. 23: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: NASA will provide an update about its Artemis III mission and its plans to land astronauts on the moon during a press conference on Friday (Oct. 23). Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: NASA will provide an update about its Artemis moon plans on Friday (Oct. 23), and you can watch it live. The news will come during a press conference at the agency's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, which starts Friday at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA. "The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and how plans to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 are progressing," NASA officials said in an Oct. 14 media advisory .
